q: Excess ethanol is heated with concentrated H₂SO₄ at about 140 °C instead of 170 °C. The main organic product is:
x: At the lower temperature with excess alcohol, two ethanol molecules lose one water molecule between them, giving diethyl ether (C₂H₅OC₂H₅). At about 170 °C with excess acid, ethene is the product.

q: Sodium ethoxide is heated with bromoethane: C₂H₅ONa + C₂H₅Br → ? + NaBr. The organic product is:
x: This is the Williamson synthesis: the ethoxide ion replaces Br in bromoethane, giving the ether C₂H₅OC₂H₅ (ethoxyethane) and NaBr.

q: The molecular formula of phenol is:
x: Phenol has an –OH group bonded directly to a benzene ring: C₆H₅OH. C₆H₅CH₂OH is benzyl alcohol and C₆H₁₁OH is cyclohexanol.

q: Propan-2-ol, CH₃CH(OH)CH₃, is classified as a:
x: The carbon carrying –OH is bonded to two other carbon atoms, so propan-2-ol is a secondary alcohol. It has only one –OH group, so it is monohydric.

q: Which pair of reagents gives methoxyethane, CH₃OC₂H₅, by the Williamson synthesis?
x: CH₃O⁻ from sodium methoxide replaces Br in C₂H₅Br, giving CH₃OC₂H₅. Bromomethane would give dimethyl ether and bromoethane with ethoxide gives diethyl ether.

q: Phenol is also known by the common name:
x: Phenol is commonly called carbolic acid. Wood spirit is methanol, picric acid is 2,4,6-trinitrophenol and glycol is ethane-1,2-diol.

q: Ethane-1,2-diol (ethylene glycol), HOCH₂CH₂OH, is an example of a:
x: It contains two –OH groups on different carbon atoms, so it is a dihydric alcohol (a diol). Glycerol, with three –OH groups, is trihydric.

q: Phenol is more acidic than ethanol mainly because:
o: Phenol has a higher molar mass
The phenoxide ion is stabilised by resonance with the benzene ring
The ethoxide ion is stabilised by resonance
x: In the phenoxide ion the negative charge spreads into the ring by resonance, which stabilises it, so phenol loses H⁺ more easily. The ethoxide ion has no such resonance.

q: The oxygen atom of the –OH group in an alcohol such as methanol is:
x: The oxygen has two bonds (to C and H) and two lone pairs, four electron pairs in all, so it is sp³ hybridised, giving a bent C–O–H arrangement.

q: Phenol is shaken with aqueous sodium hydroxide. The products are:
o: No products, as no reaction occurs
x: Phenol is acidic enough to be neutralised by NaOH: C₆H₅OH + NaOH → C₆H₅ONa + H₂O. Hydrogen is formed only with sodium metal.

q: Ethanol (M = 46) boils at 78 °C, while propane (M = 44) boils at −42 °C. The main reason is that ethanol:
x: The –OH groups of neighbouring ethanol molecules hydrogen bond to each other, and extra energy is needed to break these. Propane has only weak London forces.

q: Which reagent gives carbon dioxide with ethanoic acid but not with phenol?
x: Phenol is a weaker acid than carbonic acid, so it cannot release CO₂ from NaHCO₃, while ethanoic acid can. Sodium metal gives hydrogen, not CO₂.

q: Which alcohol is the least soluble in water?
x: All alcohols hydrogen bond with water through –OH, but the non-polar alkyl part grows with chain length. Hexan-1-ol has the largest hydrocarbon part, so it is the least soluble.

q: The compound CH₃C₆H₄OH in which the –CH₃ group is next to the –OH group is named:
x: Numbering starts at the carbon carrying –OH (C-1); the adjacent carbon is C-2, so it is 2-methylphenol (o-cresol). Benzyl alcohol is C₆H₅CH₂OH.

q: When a small piece of sodium is added to ethanol, the gas given off is:
x: 2C₂H₅OH + 2Na → 2C₂H₅ONa + H₂. Sodium replaces the hydrogen of the –OH group, forming sodium ethoxide and hydrogen gas.

q: Which of the following is NOT a phenol?
x: In C₆H₅CH₂OH (benzyl alcohol) the –OH is on a CH₂ side-chain carbon, not on the ring, so it is an aromatic alcohol. The others have –OH directly on the benzene ring.

q: Ethanol reacts with phosphorus pentachloride (PCl₅). The products are:
x: C₂H₅OH + PCl₅ → C₂H₅Cl + POCl₃ + HCl. H₃PO₃ is a product with PCl₃, and SO₂ is a product with thionyl chloride.

q: Lucas reagent, used to tell primary, secondary and tertiary alcohols apart, is a solution of:
x: Lucas reagent is concentrated HCl with anhydrous zinc chloride; it turns alcohols into insoluble chloroalkanes, seen as cloudiness at different speeds. Iodine with NaOH is the iodoform test, and acidified dichromate is the oxidation test, the reagents most often confused with it.

q: Four isomeric alcohols are warmed separately with acidified K₂Cr₂O₇. The orange colour stays orange (no green colour forms) only with:
x: Dichromate is reduced to green Cr³⁺ only when the alcohol is oxidised, which needs a hydrogen on the carbon carrying –OH. 2-Methylpropan-2-ol, (CH₃)₃COH, is tertiary and has none, so no change. Butan-2-ol is secondary and is oxidised to butanone, the tempting slip.

q: Which reagent gives a yellow precipitate with ethanol but not with methanol?
x: The iodoform test needs a CH₃CH(OH)– group (or CH₃CO–); ethanol has it and gives yellow CHI₃, while methanol does not. Sodium, dichromate and PCl₅ react with both alcohols, so they cannot tell them apart.

q: 0.1 mol of an alcohol reacts with excess sodium and gives 3.36 dm³ of hydrogen at STP (molar volume 22.4 dm³ mol⁻¹). The number of –OH groups in one molecule of the alcohol is:
x: 3.36 ÷ 22.4 = 0.15 mol H₂, which contains 0.30 mol H atoms. Each –OH gives one H atom (2ROH → 2RONa + H₂), so 0.30 ÷ 0.1 = 3 –OH groups, as in glycerol. Forgetting that each H₂ molecule needs two –OH groups gives 1.5, which points to the tempting 1 or 2.

q: Phenol is heated with zinc dust. The organic product is:
x: Zinc dust removes the oxygen: C₆H₅OH + Zn → C₆H₆ + ZnO. This reduction shows phenol contains a benzene ring. Cyclohexanol would need hydrogenation of the ring with H₂ and nickel, the tempting slip.

q: Which is the correct order of decreasing acidity?
x: Phenols are more acidic than alcohols because the phenoxide ion is resonance-stabilised. An electron-withdrawing –NO₂ at position 4 spreads the negative charge further and raises acidity; an electron-donating –CH₃ lowers it. Treating –CH₃ as acid-strengthening reverses the order of the substituted phenols.

q: A few drops of neutral iron(III) chloride solution are added to aqueous phenol. The observation is:
x: Phenol forms a violet complex with Fe³⁺, a standard test for phenols. The white precipitate comes from bromine water, and CO₂ is given by carboxylic acids with carbonate, not by phenol, which is too weak an acid.

q: Phenol reacts with dilute nitric acid at room temperature. The main products are:
x: The –OH group strongly activates the ring and directs to ortho and para positions, so even dilute HNO₃ nitrates phenol, giving a mixture of 2- and 4-nitrophenol. Picric acid (2,4,6-trinitrophenol) needs concentrated HNO₃, and the meta product would need a meta-directing group.

q: 9.4 g of phenol reacts completely with excess bromine water. What mass of white precipitate forms? (C₆H₅OH = 94 g mol⁻¹, Br = 80)
x: Phenol gives 2,4,6-tribromophenol: C₆H₅OH + 3Br₂ → C₆H₂Br₃OH + 3HBr. Mr = 72 + 2 + 240 + 17 = 331; 9.4 ÷ 94 = 0.1 mol, so 0.1 × 331 = 33.1 g. Assuming monobromination, as for benzene, gives 17.3 g.

q: To prepare 2-methoxy-2-methylpropane, CH₃OC(CH₃)₃, by Williamson's synthesis in good yield, the best reagents are:
x: Williamson's synthesis is an SN2 attack of an alkoxide on a haloalkane, so the halide should be the unhindered methyl one. A strong base like CH₃O⁻ with the tertiary halide (CH₃)₃CBr mainly eliminates HBr, giving 2-methylpropene, the tempting reversed pair. Mixed acid dehydration gives a mixture of ethers and alkenes.

q: Ethoxyethane (Mr 74) boils at 35 °C, whereas its isomer butan-1-ol (Mr 74) boils at 117 °C. The main reason is that:
o: Ethoxyethane has the larger molar mass
Ether molecules cannot form hydrogen bonds with each other, as they have no O–H group
Butan-1-ol has ionic bonds between its molecules
x: Both have the same Mr, so the difference is in intermolecular forces: butan-1-ol molecules hydrogen-bond through O–H, while ether molecules have only dipole–dipole and London forces. The C–O–C ether is bent and slightly polar, so 'non-polar' is the tempting but wrong reason.

q: Ethoxyethane is about as soluble in water as butan-1-ol, even though ether molecules do not hydrogen-bond with each other. This is because:
o: Ethoxyethane reacts with water to form ethanol
The C–H bonds of the ether form hydrogen bonds with water
The ether oxygen has lone pairs that accept hydrogen bonds from water molecules
x: Hydrogen bonding needs an H on O, N or F on one molecule and a lone pair on the other; water supplies the H and the ether oxygen supplies the lone pair. Ethers are not hydrolysed by water, and C–H hydrogens do not form hydrogen bonds.

q: Ethoxyethane is heated with excess concentrated hydriodic acid, HI. The final products are:
x: HI first cleaves the C–O–C bond: C₂H₅OC₂H₅ + HI → C₂H₅I + C₂H₅OH. With excess hot HI the ethanol also reacts, so overall C₂H₅OC₂H₅ + 2HI → 2C₂H₅I + H₂O. Ethanol plus iodoethane is the product with one mole of cold HI, the tempting slip.

q: Methoxybenzene, C₆H₅OCH₃, is heated with concentrated HI. The products are:
x: I⁻ attacks the methyl carbon by SN2; it cannot attack the ring carbon, whose C–O bond is strengthened by resonance with the ring and which cannot be approached from the back. So the O stays on the ring as phenol, and phenol is not converted further to iodobenzene. Splitting the other way gives the tempting iodobenzene and methanol.

q: Ethanol, C₂H₅OH, and methoxymethane, CH₃OCH₃, have the same molecular formula C₂H₆O. They are:
x: Both are C₂H₆O, but one is an alcohol and the other an ether, so their functional groups differ. Chain isomers differ in the carbon skeleton and position isomers in where the same group sits; neither describes an alcohol–ether pair.

q: Dry ethoxyethane is the usual solvent for preparing Grignard reagents. The main reason is that it:
o: Reacts with magnesium to start the reaction
Has no acidic hydrogen to destroy the reagent, and its oxygen lone pairs stabilise the magnesium
Is a strong acid that activates the haloalkane
Contains water that dissolves the magnesium
x: Grignard reagents are destroyed by anything with an O–H or N–H hydrogen, giving an alkane. Ethers are unreactive towards Mg and RMgX, and the ether oxygen coordinates to Mg, keeping the reagent in solution. Water must be excluded, so the last option is the opposite of the truth.

q: How many ethers (structural isomers only) have the molecular formula C₄H₁₀O?
x: The ethers are CH₃OCH₂CH₂CH₃ (1-methoxypropane), CH₃OCH(CH₃)₂ (2-methoxypropane) and C₂H₅OC₂H₅ (ethoxyethane), so 3. Forgetting the branched methoxy compound gives 2, and counting the four butanols as well gives 7.

q: Ethoxyethane does not mix with water in all proportions, yet it dissolves in cold concentrated sulphuric acid. This is because:
o: The acid oxidises the ether to ethanoic acid
The acid dehydrates the ether to ethene
The ether oxygen is protonated by the acid, forming a soluble oxonium salt
Ethoxyethane is a stronger acid than H₂SO₄
x: The lone pair on the ether oxygen accepts H⁺ from the strong acid: (C₂H₅)₂O + H₂SO₄ → (C₂H₅)₂OH⁺ HSO₄⁻, an ionic oxonium salt that dissolves. Here the ether acts as a weak base, not an acid; oxidation and dehydration need heating.
